newsitem.title: USA: Industry sees modest slowdown in US housing starts.
newsitem.headline: Industry sees modest slowdown in US housing starts.

text.p: A moderate slowdown in the housing sector is underway, but housing starts for all of 1996 should be up eight percent from last year, David Seiders, chief economist of the National Association of Home Builders said Wednesday.

"Data on the housing sector have been mixed for the third quarter, but the balance of evidence suggests that a moderate slowdown of housing market activity is now underway," Seiders said in an outlook prepared for a construction conference.
Despite a projected slowdown in the second half, housing starts should be about 1.46 million units for 1996, he said. That forecast was higher than NAHB's original 1996 estimate.
Long-term mortgage rates were expected to hover around 7.9 percent during the second half of the year, Seiders said.
The economy was likely to slow down during the second half of 1996, inflation was expected to be stable, and the Federal Reserve was not expected to raise interest rates, he said.

"We expect economic growth to slow down further in the fourth quarter, but the chances of falling into the red zone (the beginnings of recession) are very small this year," he said. NAHB forecast housing starts would decline in 1997 by about seven percent to 1.35 million units.

The projected drop in housing starts next year was due to expectations of about two percent economic growth and an increase in the unemployment rate to a projected 5.7 percent from 5.4 percent in 1996.
Inflation was expected to hold around three percent and long-term interest rates were forecast to drift down in 1997.

Seiders warned that an "even-keel" economy could be derailed by unforeseen shocks. In such a case, the Fed would likely choose to make further gains against inflation rather than rushing to the rescue with lower rates, he said.

The housing sector is faced with high and volatile lumber prices, Seiders said. "Deepening problems on the supply side of the U.S. lumber market, including the effects of the recent U.S.-Canadian lumber agreement, ensure that price volatility will continue in the future," he said.

If either political party gains control of both Congress and the White House, forecasts may need to be revised, Seiders said. "A Republican takeover would prompt the greatest change to the outlook, particularly if the key elements of Bob Dole's tax plan were enacted in 1997, but that's certainly a long shot," he said.
